column4: This is the only other imperative use of the section's rebuking verb: وَلَا تَنْهَرْهُمَا forbids scolding aged parents and replaces it with قَوْلًا كَرِيمًا, making gentle speech the positive counterpart.
After 17:23 forbids verbal harshness, the body answers with وَاخْفِضْ لَهُمَا جَنَاحَ الذُّلِّ مِنَ الرَّحْمَةِ; one lowers oneself mercifully rather than lowering another through qahr.
When material help must be deferred, فَقُلْ لَهُمْ قَوْلًا مَيْسُورًا requires an easy, consoling word; it directly joins the section's giving hand to its speaking tongue.
قَوْلٌ مَعْرُوفٌ وَمَغْفِرَةٌ is better than charity followed by hurt, so a soft word can outweigh a gift made into a second form of hard handling.
At an estate division, relatives, orphans, and the poor receive both provision and قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا; the ayah enacts the section's paired material and verbal gentleness.
Divine mercy made the Prophet لِنْتَ لَهُمْ; the stated alternative, being harsh and hard-hearted, would scatter people from around him.
Even Pharaoh is to be addressed with قَوْلًا لَيِّنًا, the clearest limit placed on the tongue's impulse to rebuke.
وَلَا تَطْرُدِ الَّذِينَ يَدْعُونَ رَبَّهُمْ directly forbids driving away socially weak believers, matching the section's rejected image of qalā as chasing a herd.
The servants of the Merciful يَمْشُونَ عَلَى الْأَرْضِ هَوْنًا and answer ignorant address with peace, uniting the section's unhurried gait and gentle tongue in one ayah.
وَاقْصِدْ فِي مَشْيِكَ وَاغْضُضْ مِنْ صَوْتِكَ pairs measured walking with a lowered voice, then contrasts the harshest voice with a donkey's bray.
Moses describes the Lord as الَّذِي أَعْطَى كُلَّ شَيْءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هَدَى, placing the section's two named roots, giving and guiding, in the same divine sequence.
God found the believers few, vulnerable, and afraid of being snatched, then فَآوَاكُمْ, strengthened them, and provided for them; shelter is the gentle answer to human domination.
فَأْوُوا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ leads immediately to promised mercy and مِرْفَقًا, a facilitated outcome; shelter, tenderness, and ease converge exactly as in the section's lexicon.
Sacrificial cattle are made serviceable, stand quietly, and then feed الْقَانِعَ وَالْمُعْتَرَّ; this concretizes both the source dictionary's yielding camel and care for one who comes asking.
After bodies shiver in awe, تَلِينُ جُلُودُهُمْ وَقُلُوبُهُمْ softens skins and hearts toward God's remembrance, giving Qur'anic form to the section's softened heart.
Orphans are to be met through reform and fraternity, and God says He could have burdened people had He willed; the ayah opposes exploitative handling with brotherly care and divine forbearance.
Those not ready to manage property are still to be fed and clothed from it and addressed with قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا, again joining provision to dignifying speech.
The covenant places good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, and the needy beside وَقُولُوا لِلنَّاسِ حُسْنًا, gathering the section's vulnerable recipients and gentle speech.
Giving remains sound only when it is not followed by reminder or injury; this supplies the rule whose verbal alternative is stated in 2:263.
Immediately after the ban on expelling worshippers in 6:52, the Prophet must greet approaching believers with peace and announce that the Lord has prescribed mercy for Himself.
Noah says وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا to elites who despise his poor followers, a direct second prohibition of the section's chasing-away image.
Noah again states وَمَا أَنَا بِطَارِدِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ, refusing to purchase elite approval by driving vulnerable believers away.
The Prophet must patiently keep himself with those who call on their Lord morning and evening and not let his eyes pass beyond them, a sustained gentle hold parallel to 6:52.
ادْفَعْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ turns hostile relation into intimate friendship; the ayah makes a better response, rather than a harder counterblow, transformative.
God tells His servants يَقُولُوا الَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ because Satan incites discord, identifying careful speech as the restraint that prevents verbal harm.
People of means must not swear to stop giving kin, the needy, and emigrants; pardon and overlooking replace the closed hand and wounded relation.
Divorced women must be housed according to means, not harmed to constrict them, and nursing arrangements settled بِمَعْرُوفٍ; shelter, provision, and humane speech oppose coercive pressure.
The well-off and constrained alike give from what God gave them, while God burdens no soul beyond His gift and promises ease after hardship.
Marriage may be retained بِمَعْرُوفٍ or released بِإِحْسَانٍ; even literal social holding and letting go are bounded by the section's gentle grip.
One who yields his face to God while doing good has اسْتَمْسَكَ بِالْعُرْوَةِ الْوُثْقَى; yielding and a secure handhold coexist without the humiliation of human qahr.
فَأَمَّا مَنْ أَعْطَى وَاتَّقَى makes the section's named giving root the first movement toward an eased path.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْيُسْرَى states the ease opened for the giver of 92:5, developing the yielding quality the section hears in أَعْطَى.
The one who يُؤْتِي مَالَهُ يَتَزَكَّى gives wealth for purification, supplying the concrete generous act that culminates in satisfaction at 92:21.
وَلَسَوْفَ يَرْضَى closely echoes the promise of future satisfaction in 93:5, while the preceding scene makes generous giving its setting.
فَإِنْ أُعْطُوا مِنْهَا رَضُوا places أُعْطُوا and رَضُوا together as in 93:5, but exposes a merely conditional contentment governed by whether people receive alms.
The better response to 9:58 is contentment with what God and His Messenger give and trust in further divine bounty, clarifying receiving without grasping resentment.
هَذَا عَطَاؤُنَا فَامْنُنْ أَوْ أَمْسِكْ names divine gift and then gives Solomon discretion to bestow or withhold, placing giving and holding in one explicit formula.
إِنَّا أَعْطَيْنَاكَ الْكَوْثَرَ is another direct divine address to the Prophet with the section's giving root, but here the gift is already emphatically bestowed.
The Lord extends support to both groups, and وَمَا كَانَ عَطَاءُ رَبِّكَ مَحْظُورًا declares His giving unconfined, the opposite of a clenched human distribution.
وَهُوَ الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ assigns the section's domination root to God and thus grounds its claim that the servant may not assume that position over the orphan.
The repeated وَهُوَ الْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ occurs amid God's guardianship until death, reinforcing divine rather than human possession of qahr.
The ark's sign includes سَكِينَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّكُمْ, giving the exact calm named by the section's dictionary gloss a divinely sent, tangible bearer.
In the exposed cave scene, God sends His سَكِينَة and unseen support; calm arrives precisely where fear and pursuit could force frantic flight.
هُوَ الَّذِي أَنْزَلَ السَّكِينَةَ فِي قُلُوبِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ locates divine calm inside hearts, the inward form of the section's gentle hold.
At the pledge beneath the tree, God knows what is in believers' hearts and sends السَّكِينَةَ عَلَيْهِمْ, joining a bodily pledge to inward composure.
Unbelievers put heated zealotry in their hearts, while God sends His sakīnah upon the Messenger and believers; the ayah explicitly stages the two opposed inner grips.
وَجَعَلَ اللَّيْلَ سَكَنًا directly interprets night through rest, matching the section's dictionary statement that the night verb سجى is stillness.
God makes night لِتَسْكُنُوا فِيهِ and day visible, restating the section's night-and-day image in functional terms.
Divine mercy makes night and day so people may rest in one and seek bounty in the other, joining repose, provision, and gratitude.
وَجَعَلْنَا نَوْمَكُمْ سُبَاتًا supplies the repose within the following night-and-day sequence.
وَجَعَلْنَا اللَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا makes night an enveloping cover rather than an abandonment, continuing the repose of 78:9.
وَجَعَلْنَا النَّهَارَ مَعَاشًا completes the calm night's counterpart with the day's livelihood, paralleling the section's paired times and comfortable life.
وَلَا تَعْجَلْ بِالْقُرْآنِ directly repeats the source dictionary's wording “do not hurry,” addressing the Prophet with restraint until revelation is completed.
لَا تُحَرِّكْ بِهِ لِسَانَكَ لِتَعْجَلَ بِهِ applies “do not hurry” to the Prophet's tongue itself, turning gentleness into measured reception and recitation.
وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَى is a divine promise to ease the Prophet toward ease, close to the section's yielding roots and unforced movement.
God does not intend hardship in purification but intends to complete نِعْمَتَهُ; ease and the section's named blessing root occur in a single purpose clause.
When God gives expansively, the human says He أَكْرَمَنِي and the ayah uses وَنَعَّمَهُ; the named softness/blessing root is tested by what follows toward the orphan.
The same person reads measured provision as humiliation, exposing the mistaken equation of a tightened livelihood with divine contempt before the orphan indictment.
وُجُوهٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ نَاعِمَةٌ gives the section's dictionary sense of the niʿmah root—soft, at ease—a bodily appearance.
لِسَعْيِهَا رَاضِيَةٌ joins satisfaction to the “soft/at-ease” faces of 88:8, echoing the gift-and-contentment movement of 93:5.
يَا أَيَّتُهَا النَّفْسُ الْمُطْمَئِنَّةُ addresses the soul defined by settled calm, the inward culmination of the section's recurrent stillness.
ارْجِعِي إِلَى رَبِّكِ رَاضِيَةً مَرْضِيَّةً joins that tranquility to mutual satisfaction, strengthening the relation between calm and contentment.
وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ commands the Prophet to embody gentleness by lowering his wing to believers.
وَاخْفِضْ جَنَاحَكَ لِمَنِ اتَّبَعَكَ repeats the lowered-wing posture for the Prophet's followers, a bodily opposite to qahr from above.
John is بَرًّا بِوَالِدَيْهِ and not جَبَّارًا عَصِيًّا; kindness to parents is explicitly opposed to tyrannical character.
Jesus says God made him dutiful to his mother and not جَبَّارًا شَقِيًّا, repeating the boundary between filial gentleness and coercive arrogance.
The Messenger is burdened by believers' suffering, deeply concerned for them, and رَءُوفٌ رَحِيمٌ, supplying the prophetic stance behind the gentle commands.
Mary is graciously accepted, made to grow well, entrusted to Zechariah, and found with provision; divine and human care enact shelter without domination.
The youths أَوَوْا إِلَى الْكَهْفِ and ask for mercy and right guidance, bringing shelter, softened divine care, and direction together.
وَآوَيْنَاهُمَا إِلَى رَبْوَةٍ ذَاتِ قَرَارٍ وَمَعِينٍ portrays divine shelter of mother and son as a settled, provisioned refuge.
آوَى إِلَيْهِ أَخَاهُ is Joseph's intimate reception of his brother; the named shelter root becomes a kinship gesture rather than mere lodging.
آوَى إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ depicts Joseph drawing his parents into his protection, meeting the parent-care scene of 17:23–24 through the section's shelter root.
The fleeing sinner would ransom even فَصِيلَتِهِ الَّتِي تُؤْوِيهِ, identifying one's close clan by its ordinary work of sheltering.
A wall preserves treasure for two orphan boys until maturity, explicitly as mercy from the Lord; unseen protection answers the orphan's vulnerability without crushing control.
Worship of God is immediately joined to good treatment of parents, kin, orphans, the needy, neighbors, travelers, and dependents, mapping the social reach of the gentle hold.
God commands justice, excellence, and giving to kin while forbidding oppression; gift and coercion are placed on opposite sides of one compact command.
True devotion includes giving loved wealth to kin, orphans, the needy, traveler, and askers, so the section's orphan and asker both meet an open hand.
The answer about spending names parents, kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers, directing material giving toward the same vulnerable relations developed in the section.
The poor are restrained enough that they do not ask people insistently; the ayah teaches the reader to recognize need before the asker must expose himself to rebuke.
وَفِي أَمْوَالِهِمْ حَقٌّ لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ makes the asker and the one unable to ask both rightful recipients, moving response beyond discretionary condescension.
Believers set aside a recognized share in their wealth, preparing the material answer to the two vulnerable recipients named in 70:25.
That recognized share is لِلسَّائِلِ وَالْمَحْرُومِ, directly converting the encounter with an asker into acknowledged right.
They feed, despite loving the food, the needy, orphan, and captive; even a captive receives the open hand rather than domination.
The feeders seek neither repayment nor thanks, removing the verbal and social pressure that can turn a gift into hard control.
فَكُّ رَقَبَةٍ makes loosening a human neck, the undoing of a hard physical hold, the first form of the steep moral path.
أَوْ إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ adds feeding under famine to the release of 90:13.
The feeding is directed to يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ, making the section's orphan a concrete recipient of costly care.
أَوْ مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ extends that care to the destitute person brought low to the dust.
The sequence culminates in mutual counsel to patience and مَرْحَمَةِ, naming mercy as the social bond behind freeing and feeding.
وَآتُوا الْيَتَامَى أَمْوَالَهُمْ commands the return of orphan property and forbids consuming it, replacing possessive seizure with faithful release.
Once orphans reach sound judgment, فَادْفَعُوا إِلَيْهِمْ أَمْوَالَهُمْ requires guardians to hand their wealth over rather than keep a controlling grip.
Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly are described as consuming fire, exposing the violent reality hidden inside exploitative guardianship.
The ruling about vulnerable women and children ends with وَأَنْ تَقُومُوا لِلْيَتَامَى بِالْقِسْطِ, requiring active justice for orphans.
Approaching orphan property is forbidden except in the best manner until maturity, placing a strict boundary around the guardian's hand.
The same “best manner until maturity” rule protects orphan property, followed by the demand to fulfill covenants.
Even a hostile polytheist who seeks protection must be granted asylum and conveyed to safety; shelter and gentle hearing cross an enemy boundary.
Giving kin, the needy, and the traveler their due supplies the material setting for the easy word commanded two ayat later in 17:28.
فَآتِ ذَا الْقُرْبَى حَقَّهُ وَالْمِسْكِينَ وَابْنَ السَّبِيلِ again frames aid as a recipient's due, not the giver's humiliating favor.
The distribution to kin, orphans, needy, and travelers is designed so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, an institutional check on the closed hand.
The assigned share of spoils includes kin, orphans, the needy, and travelers, protecting their provision even amid the hard scene of war.
Pharaoh's وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَاهِرُونَ follows his threat to kill sons and spare women, displaying human qahr as domination from above and degradation in practice.
فَذَلِكَ الَّذِي يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ pictures the orphan being shoved away, the stark physical opposite of the ban on crushing him.
The one who shoves the orphan also fails to urge feeding the poor, joining a hard hand to withheld provision.
كَلَّا بَلْ لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ corrects the wealth-based reasoning of 89:15–16 by making treatment of the orphan the test of bestowed ease.
وَلَا تَحَاضُّونَ عَلَى طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ extends that failure from the orphan to the unfed poor.
وَتَأْكُلُونَ التُّرَاثَ أَكْلًا لَمًّا shows the grasping appetite that accompanies neglect of orphan and poor.
وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا names attachment to accumulated wealth as the inner hard grip behind the preceding failures.
عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّى records a facial and bodily withdrawal, the opposite of a gentle reception for one who approaches.
أَنْ جَاءَهُ الْأَعْمَى identifies the disregarded visitor as a blind man, sharpening the vulnerable-asker parallel.
The overlooked visitor might have purified himself, showing what is lost when surface status controls the response.
He might have remembered and benefited from the reminder; his request carried spiritual value rather than nuisance.
أَمَّا مَنِ اسْتَغْنَى turns to the self-sufficient person, establishing the social contrast governing the mistaken attention.
فَأَنْتَ لَهُ تَصَدَّى says the self-sufficient one received deliberate attention, unlike the vulnerable visitor.
The Prophet bears no blame if that self-sufficient hearer does not purify himself, removing the rationale for preferential pursuit.
وَأَمَّا مَنْ جَاءَكَ يَسْعَى returns to the seeker who came striving, a concrete counterpart to the section's sāʾil.
وَهُوَ يَخْشَى reveals the seeker's inward reverence and further reverses the status judgment.
فَأَنْتَ عَنْهُ تَلَهَّى completes the rebuke: distraction from the earnest vulnerable seeker is itself the failed hold.
وَأَمَّا مَنْ بَخِلَ وَاسْتَغْنَى reverses the giving of 92:5 through withholding and felt self-sufficiency.
فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ لِلْعُسْرَى makes the withholder's destination “difficulty,” the formal opposite of the giver's ease in 92:7.
وَأَعْطَى قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَى uses the named giving root for a small gift abruptly stopped, showing a hand that opens only to harden again.
فَتَعَاطَى فَعَقَرَ uses a different stem of the section's named ع ط و root for the culprit's reaching/undertaking before hamstringing the she-camel, a violent reversal of yielding gift.
حَتَّى يُعْطُوا الْجِزْيَةَ عَنْ يَدٍ وَهُمْ صَاغِرُونَ places the named giving root in a compelled political submission, a hard boundary to the source dictionary's willing, unresisting yield.
The claim that God's hand is fettered is answered with بَلْ يَدَاهُ مَبْسُوطَتَانِ يُنْفِقُ كَيْفَ يَشَاءُ, making closed and open hands explicit images of withholding and giving.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit; the ayah gives the section's “hold” a measured ethical boundary.
Hypocrites وَيَقْبِضُونَ أَيْدِيَهُمْ, closing their hands while promoting wrong, a bodily image of withheld generosity.
وَلَا تُمْسِكُوهُنَّ ضِرَارًا forbids retaining wives in order to harm and transgress; literal holding becomes unlawful when used as pressure.
Compulsory possession of women and constricting them to recover gifts are forbidden, then وَعَاشِرُوهُنَّ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ supplies the humane alternative.
The coming community is أَذِلَّةٍ عَلَى الْمُؤْمِنِينَ أَعِزَّةٍ عَلَى الْكَافِرِينَ, marking a contextual boundary between humble tenderness and firmness.
أَشِدَّاءُ عَلَى الْكُفَّارِ رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ similarly distinguishes severity toward hostile opposition from mercy within the believing community.
The Prophet is commanded to strive against disbelievers and hypocrites and be stern with them, a context-specific boundary to the gentleness commanded in 3:159.
The repeated command to be stern toward disbelievers and hypocrites prevents the section's softness from being read as the erasure of every moral boundary.
Prophetic wives are told not to be yieldingly soft in speech where it could invite diseased desire, but to speak appropriately; softness itself needs a moral setting.
Believers must not insult rival objects of worship lest others insult God ignorantly, placing restraint on harsh speech even amid theological opposition.
Retaliation may match the harm suffered, yet patience is expressly better; the ayah draws a boundary around force after the gentle invitation of 16:125.
A wrong may receive an equal response, but pardon and reconciliation bring reward from God, balancing justice with the gentler release of grievance.
Hatred of a people must not drive believers away from justice, so hostility cannot license the dominating or demeaning grip.
Hearts become like stones or harder, while even stones split, release water, or fall in awe; the image exposes a hardness less responsive than rock.
Covenant-breaking brings hardened hearts and distorted words, yet the Prophet is told to pardon and overlook, placing hard interior and gentle response together.
When wrongdoers sense divine might, إِذَا هُمْ مِنْهَا يَرْكُضُونَ pictures frantic running in defeat, the exact motion opposed by the source dictionary's calm gait.
لَا تَرْكُضُوا commands those fleeing judgment not to run, sharply reversing their defeated haste and echoing the section's “do not hurry.”
After Moses reaches to seize a man, he is accused of wanting to be جَبَّارًا فِي الْأَرْضِ; the scene ties a grasping hand to tyrannical domination.
وَإِذَا بَطَشْتُمْ بَطَشْتُمْ جَبَّارِينَ names violent seizing performed as tyrants, perhaps the clearest nonlexical picture of the section's hard hand.
فَاسْتَخَفَّ قَوْمَهُ فَأَطَاعُوهُ shows Pharaoh making his people contemptibly light until they obey, matching qahr's combination of domination and degradation.
Pharaoh threatens to cut opposing hands and feet and crucify the magicians, displaying the coercive hand behind his claim to mastery.
The same threat of crosswise amputation and crucifixion makes Pharaoh's qahr bodily and punitive.
Pharaoh again threatens crosswise amputation and crucifixion when belief escapes his control, a repeated hard grasp on conscience and body.
وَمَا أَنْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِجَبَّارٍ denies that the Prophet is a coercive dominator and directs him instead to remind through the Qur'an.
فَذَكِّرْ إِنَّمَا أَنْتَ مُذَكِّرٌ defines the messenger's task as reminder rather than crushing control.
لَسْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِمُصَيْطِرٍ explicitly denies mastery over hearers, completing 88:21's boundary on prophetic force.
Would the Prophet compel people until they became believers? The rhetorical question rejects coercion even in pursuit of faith.
Noah's son says سَآوِي إِلَى جَبَلٍ, seeking self-shelter in a mountain, but the flood reveals that refuge without divine mercy cannot hold.
نِعْمَةٌ مِنْ رَبِّهِ catches Jonah before he is cast onto the open shore blameworthy, making divine favor a preserving hold against rejection.
Noah is called mad and وَازْدُجِرَ, “rebuked/driven off” with the same z-j-r wording used in the source dictionary to define harsh nahr.
When fear passes, hypocrites سَلَقُوكُمْ بِأَلْسِنَةٍ حِدَادٍ, lashing believers with sharp tongues; the hard tongue becomes almost a weapon.
Ridicule, mutual defamation, and insulting names are forbidden, specifying ordinary verbal forms of demeaning another.
Woe is pronounced on every slanderer and mocker, the character built from the harsh tongue the section forbids.
Joseph asks whether scattered lords are better than Allah الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ; the named root is again a divine title, not a human license.
After contrasting creator with powerless partners, the ayah names God الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, reinforcing the section's Creator-servant boundary around qahr.
On the transformed earth all emerge before اللَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ; universal exposure gives the divine title its eschatological setting.
The Prophet is told to announce that there is no deity but اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, joining warning speech to exclusive divine qahr.
The rejection of divine offspring closes with سُبْحَانَهُ هُوَ اللَّهُ الْوَاحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ, again reserving the title for God.
On the day all are exposed, sovereignty is declared to belong to اللَّهِ الْوَاحِدِ الْقَهَّارِ, placing irresistible domination at final judgment.
وَالشَّمْسِ وَضُحَاهَا repeats the section's ḍuḥā word as the sun's brightness, anchoring its secondary “do not hurry” reading in the word's ordinary luminous scene.
وَالنَّهَارِ إِذَا جَلَّاهَا develops the daylight side of 91:1 and parallels the section's opening movement from ḍuḥā.
وَاللَّيْلِ إِذَا يَغْشَاهَا sets covering night against revealed day, a second oath-pair that helps distinguish visual covering from the section's still night.
وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَاهَا uses the named root for the earth's brought-forth daylight, another Qur'anic sense beside the source dictionary's gentle, unhurried branch.
Night is made so people may rest and day to give sight, repeating the quiet-night relation that the section hears in سجى.
God makes night for rest and day for sight, then describes His bounty, joining repose to divine favor.
Night is clothing, sleep repose, and day a rising, giving the section's still night an enveloping and restorative interpretation.
The question asks who besides God could bring a night in which people rest if day were perpetual, making stillness a necessary mercy.
Sleep by night and day and seeking divine bounty are both signs, loosening the rigid equation of night with rest while preserving repose and provision.
The Messenger must endure with the resolve of earlier messengers and وَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلْ لَهُمْ, applying the source's “do not hurry” to judgment against opponents.
فَلَا تَعْجَلْ عَلَيْهِمْ restrains haste toward deniers because their term is already counted, a judicial form of the section's unhurried posture.
Humanity is created of haste and told فَلَا تَسْتَعْجِلُونِ; this names the temperament against which the section's lexical softness is heard.
The Prophet must bear what opponents say and leave them هَجْرًا جَمِيلًا, answering verbal injury with patient, dignified disengagement.
فَاصْفَحِ الصَّفْحَ الْجَمِيلَ commands a beautiful overlooking, a deliberate release rather than a retaliatory hard hold.
Take pardon, command what is recognized, and turn from the ignorant: the ayah gives a compact practice for refusing the rebuking tongue.
Invitation is to proceed with wisdom, good instruction, and argument بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ, specifying the verbal manner developed in 20:44.
Disputation with the People of the Book must use what is best, except toward those who act unjustly, a stated boundary for gentle address.
ادْفَعْ بِالَّتِي هِيَ أَحْسَنُ directs the Prophet to meet evil with what is better, turning resistance away from matching hardness.
When believers hear vain or hurtful talk, they turn away and say peace rather than return the verbal aggression.
فَاصْفَحْ عَنْهُمْ وَقُلْ سَلَامٌ joins release of grievance to a peaceful word, a concise opposite to nahr.
Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet's or address him loudly like one another, setting a limit on forceful vocal manner.
Those who lower their voices before God's Messenger are praised, giving the preceding prohibition a positive form of vocal restraint.
Livestock carry burdens to places people could reach only with severe hardship, and the Lord is described as compassionate and merciful; serviceable animals embody softened difficulty.

God tells the Prophet to leave affluent deniers, أُولِي النَّعْمَةِ, to Him and grant them a little respite; luxury from the named root is paired with unhurried judgment.

فَهُوَ فِي عِيشَةٍ رَاضِيَةٍ repeats the pleasing life, a concise Qur'anic counterpart to the dictionary's ease and repose in living.
